titleText.es: ¡Quizás escriba algún día un artículo en la Wikipedia sobre este lugar! Espera, maldita sea, investigación original.
titleText.en: Maybe someday I will write a Wikipedia article about this place! Wait, damn it—original research.
titleText.noteEn: Wikipedia articles are expected to summarize published sources rather than introduce an editor's own original research.

applications.explanationEn: La and the feminine ending on nuestra agree with the feminine thing that the phrase leaves unstated.
Del contains de plus the masculine article el, and nuestro has the matching masculine ending for the omitted thing.
Se stays with corresponde, while con introduces the information used for the match; esto is the thing being compared.

regions.labelEs: AYUDA, POR FAVOR. CREO QUE ME HE PERDIDO.

applications.explanationEn: Ayuda is the informal singular command form used to ask one person for help.
Por and favor form the fixed politeness expression used with the request.
He is the present helper form for the speaker, and perdido is perder's unchanged completed-action form.
Me identifies the speaker as the person who became lost, and perdido supplies the completed action; he between them marks the present perfect.

cards.answerEn: In special relativity, observers moving relative to one another can measure different elapsed times; a moving clock is measured as running more slowly.
cards.noteEn: The effect becomes substantial only at speeds that are a significant fraction of the speed of light.

cards.answerEn: each other; marks an action exchanged by two or more subjects

cards.promptEs: se + verbo plural: el uno al otro
cards.questionEn: How can you say that two or more people do the same action to each other?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a verb whose form matches the plural group doing the action.
cards.noteEn: With a plural subject, se can show that the members exchange an action: se escriben can mean “they write to each other.” Se can have other uses too, so the surrounding meaning tells you whether the action is reciprocal.

example.es: Ana y Luis se escriben cada semana.
example.en: Ana and Luis write to each other every week.

cards.noteEn: Sendos comes before a plural masculine noun and says that each previously named person or thing has one of that noun. The feminine form is sendas. It does not simply mean “two” or “both.”

example.es: Ana y Luis llevan sendas mochilas.
example.en: Ana and Luis each carry a backpack.

cards.answerEn: at (introducing a measured distance, speed, or rate)
In physics, c is the speed of light in a vacuum; 0,2 c means twenty percent of that speed.
cards.noteEn: The decimal comma in 0,2 is the Spanish notation for 0.2.

cards.answerEn: ugh; darn (a mild frustrated reaction, especially in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Jo is a mild exclamation of annoyance, disappointment, or surprise. It does not literally name a sigh, even when it replaces a written sigh in a translation.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: With formal usted, su can mean “your.” The same form can also mean “his,” “her,” or “their,” so context identifies the owner.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; Spanish commonly uses un before a percentage
cards.noteEn: A percentage can behave like a masculine quantity in Spanish, so it often follows un: un 20%. Natural English normally says only “20%,” without “a” or “one.”

example.es: Un 20% de los asientos está libre.
example.en: Twenty percent of the seats are free.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; the article used before nuestra (“ours”)
cards.noteEn: When a feminine noun has already been named, la can introduce a possessive form that means “the one belonging to us.” La matches the omitted feminine noun; natural English usually says only “ours.”

example.es: Su bicicleta es azul; la nuestra es roja.
example.en: Her bicycle is blue; ours is red.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “the one that is mine, yours, or ours” without repeating a noun?
cards.answerEn: Use el, la, los, or las before a possessive form such as mío, tuya, suyo, or nuestro.
cards.noteEn: This pattern points back to a previously named thing: la nuestra means “the feminine one that is ours,” while el nuestro means “the masculine one that is ours.” The article and the ending match that omitted thing, not its owner. After de + el, Spanish contracts the two words to del, as in del nuestro. For a simple statement of ownership after ser, the article is normally absent: Es nuestro means “It is ours.”

example.es: Tu mesa es grande, pero la nuestra es pequeña.
example.en: Your table is large, but ours is small.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: of the; combines de + el before nuestro (“ours”)
cards.noteEn: Spanish always contracts de + el to del. Here el introduces a masculine possessive form that replaces an already named noun, so del nuestro can contribute the meaning “of ours.”

example.es: El motor de tu coche es más potente que el del nuestro.
example.en: Your car's engine is more powerful than ours.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of corresponderse con (“to match”)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one result, description, or set of facts matches another?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of corresponderse followed by con and the thing it matches.
cards.noteEn: Keep the short se with the changed form of corresponder: se corresponde for one thing and se corresponden for several. Con introduces the other information used for the comparison.

example.es: El dibujo se corresponde con la descripción.

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.
Sus is used before plural things that are owned. It agrees with what is owned, not with the owner; with usted, it can mean formal “your.”

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of por favor (“please”)

cards.noteEn: Por favor makes a request more polite. It can appear before or after the request.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets lost?
cards.answerEn: Use perder with a matching short word such as me, te, or se: me pierdo, te pierdes, se pierde.
cards.noteEn: Perder by itself usually means “to lose something.” Perderse describes the person becoming lost, so the short word changes with that person. In a completed-action form such as me he perdido, me still identifies the person who became lost.

example.en: We got lost in the park.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?
